newsitem.title: KENYA: Joint U.N.-OAU Great Lakes envoy a man of principle. [CORRECTED 09:41 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Joint U.N.-OAU Great Lakes envoy a man of principle. [CORRECTED 09:41 GMT]

text.p: Mohamed Sahnoun, the Algerian diplomat chosen to tackle the spreading conflict in Africa's Great Lakes region (corrects from "conflict"), has shown in the past he is willing to put principle before his career.
Sahnoun was named in New York on Wednesday and will be the first joint special representative of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
A slight man with a good sense of humour, Sahnoun showed his steel in 1992 when he stood up to former U.N. secretary-general Boutros Boutros-Ghali, resigning as special representative in Somalia.
"He is recognised by almost everybody as a very skilled diplomat and negotiator," a senior official at OAU headquarters in Ethiopia told Reuters.
Sahnoun lasted exactly six months in Somalia. He felt obliged to resign after Boutros rebuked him for saying the U.N. was slow reacting to famine in the Horn of Africa country.
Sahnoun's independent and anti-bureaucratic style annoyed U.N. functionaries but was admired by many Somalis, aid workers and journalists.

It may have been coincidental but after his abrupt departure Somalia's slide into anarchy accelerated. Hugely costly and misguided military operations by the United States and the U.N. led to bloodshed and ended in ignominious retreat in 1995.
Sahnoun watched from the sidelines and published a memoir to highlight policy failures and defend his record.
His latest challenge is even tougher.
The poison in relations between the Tutsi and Hutu tribes lies at the heart of a spreading conflict.
There is civil war in eastern Zaire, ethnic war in Burundi and collective trauma in Rwanda after the 1994 genocide of up to 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
These conflicts have spawned millions of refugees and displaced people, a mini-arms race and deep hostilities between regional leaders.

Spelling out Sahnoun's super-human mandate, new U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan said he would promote peace, especially in eastern Zaire and Burundi, prepare an international conference on the entire region, direct U.N. political activities and coordinate its aid.
Sahnoun seemed to have driven a hard bargain to get unprecedented back-up.
Annan said the envoy would need an aircraft and communications at his Nairobi base and establish sub-offices in the capitals of Burundi, Rwanda and Zaire.

Sahnoun's negotiating skills will first have to be deployed working out relations with the plethora of special envoys already in the Great Lakes countries, sent by the United Nations, the OAU, the European Union, the United States, Belgium, South Africa and Kenya.
Their combined efforts have failed to prevent the crisis escalating steadily. All-out war in Zaire is the next threat.
Sahnoun will be the first envoy to report to two very different organisations. The U.N. has a vast and big-spending bureaucracy while the OAU is small and hard-up.
"The rationale is to enhance cooperation between the two organisations and to forge a new partnership," an OAU official said.
The two bodies fell out publicly late last year when the OAU accused the U.N. of ignoring Africa when key decisions were taken after the rebellion in eastern Zaire.
France has sharply different views on the Great Lakes crisis than two other permanent members of the Security Council, the United States and Britain.
Africa is even more split over the Hutu-Tutsi conflict, both because of ethnic links and between French-and English-speaking countries.
Most diplomats and aid agency sources in Nairobi predicted that Sahnoun would report principally to Kofi Annan.
"I imagine he'll just keep the OAU informed," one senior aid worker said.
Asked if Sahnoun would receive two salaries, an OAU official replied: "No, just one. And the richer organisation (U.N.) will pay it."

Sahnoun spent the past five years as a freelance mediator based in Paris, working for U.N. and private agencies on conflict resolution. He helped defuse the militia war in Congo in 1993 and 1994 on behalf of the OAU, which he served as deputy secretary-general from 1964 to 1973.
He has been Algeria's ambassador to the United Nations, the United States, Germany and France and worked for the Arab League.
